slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: "I pushed, so the release tag is on the server." Root cause: a push sends tags only when asked; the branch update does not carry them.
Comparing a tag's ID with a commit ID and finding a mismatch. Root cause: the ref of an annotated tag holds the ID of the tag object; the commit is the peeled value, ^{}.
Finding the newest release with plain git tag | tail -1. Root cause: the default order is byte order, in which v1.10.0 sorts before v1.2.0.
git push --tags from a working clone. Root cause: it sends every tag you have, including private and temporary ones.
Deleting a tag on the server and assuming it is gone. Root cause: every clone holds its own copy, a plain fetch never removes it, and anyone's git push --tags brings it back.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. An ML team tags the commit that produced each published model with an annotated tag such as model/reranker/2026-09-07, and writes the evaluation run ID into the message.

The team's release script uses git push --follow-tags, so the annotated release tag goes with the branch and the engineers' private lightweight tags, for bisecting and for marking a canary, stay on their machines.
Your turn. Do Lab 13.1, "Three kinds of tag", in lab-manual/m13-tags-versions.md.

The challenge is Exercise 13.5, Level 2, command prediction, "What a tag name resolves to", in exercises/m11-m15-investigation-recovery.md.

beats.text: That question comes from a CTO in a release week, and it sounds like a question about containers. It's a question about tags.
beats.tele: That question comes from a CTO in a release week, and it sounds like a question about containers. It's a question about tags.

beats.text: To answer it you need three facts that most engineers have never had to state. A tag is a ref, a name that holds an object ID, and every clone holds its own copy of it. Some tags are only a ref, and some are a ref plus an object. And tags don't travel the way branches do. A push, which sends your work to a server, doesn't send them unless asked. A fetch, which downloads from it, never updates one you already have.

A fetch, which downloads from it, never updates one you already have.

An annotated tag points at a tag object that names the commit and records who tagged it, when and why. On screen, two tags from today's demo sit on one commit. What differs is behind the name.

beats.text: A signed tag is an annotated tag whose text ends in a signature. So there are three kinds and two mechanisms: a bare ref, or a ref plus an object. Signatures have their own videos later. Today the signed tag is "an annotated tag with a signature block in its message".
beats.tele: A signed tag is an annotated tag whose text ends in a signature. So there are three kinds and two mechanisms: a bare ref, or a ref plus an object. Signatures have their own videos later. Today the signed tag is "an annotated tag with a signature block in its message".

beats.text: Getting from the tag object to the commit is called peeling. v1.0.0^{commit} follows tag objects until it reaches a commit. v1.0.0^{}, with empty braces, follows them until it reaches anything that isn't a tag. Commands that want a commit, such as git log v1.0.0, peel for you.
beats.tele: Getting from the tag object to the commit is called peeling. `v1.0.0^{commit}` follows tag objects until it reaches a commit. `v1.0.0^{}`, with empty braces, follows them until it reaches anything that isn't a tag. Commands that want a commit, such as `git log v1.0.0`, peel for you.

beats.text: Inside the dot git folder, git tag -a writes one object and one ref. No reflog is written for tags unless core.logAllRefUpdates is always. HEAD, the index and the working tree aren't involved.
beats.tele: Inside the dot git folder, `git tag -a` writes one object and one ref. No reflog is written for tags unless `core.logAllRefUpdates` is `always`. HEAD, the index and the working tree aren't involved.

beats.text: Which kind when? The manual's rule: annotated tags for releases, lightweight tags for private or temporary labels. git describe ignores lightweight tags by default for that reason. An annotated tag also answers "who released this, and when", which the last commit's author line can't.
beats.tele: Which kind when? The manual's rule: annotated tags for releases, lightweight tags for private or temporary labels. `git describe` ignores lightweight tags by default for that reason. An annotated tag also answers "who released this, and when", which the last commit's author line can't.

beats.text: Listing. git tag lists in byte order, which is wrong for version numbers. --sort=version:refname compares the numeric parts as numbers. It still lists a pre-release after its release, because the suffix makes a longer string. versionsort.suffix names the suffixes that sort before the bare version.

It still lists a pre-release after its release, because the suffix makes a longer string. `versionsort.suffix` names the suffixes that sort before the bare version.

beats.text: Filters select by history, not by name. On screen, the tags of the second demo, each on its commit. --contains answers "which releases include this fix", and --merged answers "which releases are in the history of this commit".

beats.text: How tags travel. Three rules.
beats.tele: How tags travel. Three rules.

beats.text: Push sends tags only when asked. git push origin <tag> publishes one. git push --follow-tags sends, with the branch, every annotated tag that points into the commits being pushed and is missing on the server. git push --tags sends every tag you have, including the private ones.
beats.tele: Push sends tags only when asked. `git push origin <tag>` publishes one. `git push --follow-tags` sends, with the branch, every annotated tag that points into the commits being pushed and is missing on the server. `git push --tags` sends every tag you have, including the private ones.

beats.text: Fetch follows tags. A fetch brings every tag that points into the history it downloads, of either kind, and never updates a tag you already have.
beats.tele: Fetch follows tags. A fetch brings every tag that points into the history it downloads, of either kind, and never updates a tag you already have.

beats.text: Deleting is per place. A tag lives in three places: your clone, the server, and every other clone. Each needs its own command.
beats.tele: Deleting is per place. A tag lives in three places: your clone, the server, and every other clone. Each needs its own command.

beats.text: When not to use a tag: as something that moves. A name that's meant to move is a branch. Watch a new commit arrive: main moves to it, and the tag stays.
beats.tele: When not to use a tag: as something that moves. A name that's meant to move is a branch. Watch a new commit arrive: `main` moves to it, and the tag stays.

beats.text: And avoid a nested tag, a tag of a tag. The textbook calls it almost always a mistake, and Git 2.55 prints a hint when you create one.
beats.tele: And avoid a nested tag, a tag of a tag. The textbook calls it almost always a mistake, and Git 2.55 prints a hint when you create one.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy uses the ledger. A lightweight tag is a sticky note on a page of the ledger. An annotated tag is a certificate that cites the page number and is filed in the ledger with a page number of its own.
beats.tele: The textbook's analogy uses the ledger. A lightweight tag is a sticky note on a page of the ledger. An annotated tag is a certificate that cites the page number and is filed in the ledger with a page number of its own.

says: git tag -a writes one object and one ref
A sticky note on the page, and a certificate that cites it

beats.text: That's why an annotated tag has two IDs to keep apart: the ID of the certificate, which is what the ref holds, and the ID of the page it cites, the commit.
beats.tele: That's why an annotated tag has two IDs to keep apart: the ID of the certificate, which is what the ref holds, and the ID of the page it cites, the commit.

says: git tag -a writes one object and one ref
A sticky note on the page, and a certificate that cites it
Two IDs: b696248 is the certificate, eb112a5 the page it cites

beats.text: The analogy breaks because nobody certifies anything unless the tag is also signed. The tagger line of an annotated tag is text supplied by whoever created it, the same as an author line.
beats.tele: The analogy breaks because nobody certifies anything unless the tag is also signed. The tagger line of an annotated tag is text supplied by whoever created it, the same as an author line.

says: git tag -a writes one object and one ref

Two IDs: b696248 is the certificate, eb112a5 the page it cites
The tagger line is text supplied by whoever created the tag

beats.text: Add one thing for travel: every clone has its own set of sticky notes and its own copies of the certificates. Handing someone the ledger doesn't hand over your notes unless you say so, and once they have a note with a given name, they keep theirs.
beats.tele: Add one thing for travel: every clone has its own set of sticky notes and its own copies of the certificates. Handing someone the ledger doesn't hand over your notes unless you say so, and once they have a note with a given name, they keep theirs.
